profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting at a mid-sized SaaS company preparing a two-sprint pilot for a new estimation practice in one product squad. The team wants to adapt ideas from Vickrey auctions and Stag Hunt game framing into its existing Agile planning process without disrupting delivery. The meeting is between the Engineering Manager and the Agile Coach to decide what the pilot will include, how it will run during sprint planning and retrospective, who will prepare materials, and what must be ready before the pilot starts next Monday. The agenda is to define the pilot format, agree on which ceremonies it touches, assign setup work, and confirm the timeline. The expected outcome is a shared plan for a lightweight pilot that can be introduced to the squad with minimal friction.

members.name: Priya Raman
members.expertise: Delivery planning, cross-functional team coordination, Agile execution in product engineering
members.background: Priya manages the Payments Platform squad and previously led rollout of estimation changes at another B2B software company where process overhead quickly triggered pushback from senior engineers.
members.private_state: She wants a pilot that is visibly low-overhead, does not slow next sprint commitment, and can be presented to leadership as a practical delivery improvement rather than an experimental process change.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' should fit entirely inside normal sprint planning with no extra standalone sessions beyond a short retrospective debrief.
If they say they will 'use Vickrey', that means borrowing the sealed-bid and reveal mechanic as a facilitation pattern, not implementing literal payoff or incentive rules.
The 'next Monday' start means the squad can begin using the new approach in planning next Monday as long as prep is finished by start-of-day local time.
A 'team brief' means a concise Confluence page and five-minute verbal intro, because engineers will resist slide decks or training workshops.

members.name: Daniel Cho
members.expertise: Agile process design, facilitation, retrospective design, organizational change adoption
members.background: Daniel supports several product teams and recently ran workshop-based experiments on decision protocols in estimation and retrospectives, emphasizing behavioral consistency over immediate delivery speed.
members.private_state: He wants the pilot to preserve the behavioral logic of the game-theoretic mechanisms strongly enough to produce meaningful observations that could later scale across teams.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot' needs enough structure to test the mechanism cleanly, which usually includes a short calibration session before the first planning meeting.
If they say they will 'use Vickrey', that implies the second-price logic or an explicit proxy for it must be present; otherwise the mechanism is just renamed planning poker.
The 'next Monday' start means all participant-facing materials should already be circulated before Monday so the team arrives primed rather than introduced on the spot.
A 'team brief' means a short facilitated training artifact set, typically slides plus examples, because people need a shared mental model before trying a new protocol.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to run a 'two-sprint pilot' for the Payments squad.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya thinks the pilot is limited to modifying the estimation moment inside regular sprint planning, plus a brief retrospective check on whether the team liked it.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel thinks the pilot includes pre-planning calibration, the planning-session mechanism itself, and a structured retrospective exercise to observe cooperation effects.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as describing the same initiative and the phrase 'two-sprint pilot' sounds complete on its own, so neither feels a need to enumerate boundaries unless someone asks directly.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they will 'use Vickrey' or a 'Vickrey-style round' in estimation.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means sealed individual estimates followed by discussion anchored on the second-highest estimate as a conversation aid, without explicit incentive semantics.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means a mechanism that preserves the informational logic of a second-price auction, such as selecting a commitment anchor based on one value while evaluating truthfulness incentives separately.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The term sounds technical and shared, and both are familiar enough with the literature to assume the other is using the same shorthand, even though they operationalize it differently.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that materials and setup should be 'ready by next Monday' so the pilot can start then.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya treats success as having the Confluence page, Jira template tweaks, and facilitator notes completed before the squad's 10:00 a.m. local sprint planning on Monday.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel treats success as having participant-facing materials distributed by end of day Friday so team members have time to absorb the concept before Monday.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In planning conversations, 'ready by Monday' often passes as an ordinary deadline phrase, and each interpretation feels professionally standard within the speaker's own workflow.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree someone should prepare a 'brief for the team' before rollout.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya expects a lightweight written brief in Confluence and a verbal intro delivered live during planning.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel expects a short slide deck with worked examples and a 20-minute facilitated walkthrough before the first estimation round.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'brief for the team' is routine and underspecified; both assume the delivery format is obvious from their own prior rollout experience, so they focus on ownership rather than method.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to land as a practical tweak, not a process experiment. For me the two-sprint pilot is just a light change inside normal sprint planning, then a quick debrief in retro to see if the team found it useful. If we can have the Confluence page, Jira tweaks, and a few facilitator notes ready before the squad's 10 a.m. planning next Monday, we're good. Anything that smells like extra sessions will trigger pushback.
turns.utterance: I'd like us to lock the format today so we can run a lightweight two-sprint pilot with Payments starting next Monday. My main goal is to keep it easy for the team to absorb and not make planning feel heavier than it already does.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a two-sprint pilot gives enough room to see whether the mechanism actually changes behavior. I want this to include the calibration before the first planning meeting, the Vickrey-style estimation itself with the core second-price logic preserved, and a structured retrospective around cooperation choices. If we say we're using Vickrey, it needs to be more than a renamed estimation ritual.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. If we do a two-sprint pilot, we can use Vickrey-style estimation in planning and bring the cooperation framing into retrospective as well, so we have a clean read on whether behavior shifts at all.

turns.inner_thought: I'm okay with the Vickrey language as long as in practice it's just a facilitation pattern inside planning: sealed estimates, quick reveal, use the anchor to guide discussion, done. I do not want to introduce incentive-rule debates or extra mechanics that lengthen commitment. Keep it inside the existing ceremony and leadership will see it as a delivery improvement.
turns.utterance: I'm fine with using Vickrey in planning as long as it comes across as a small adjustment inside the existing ceremony rather than a new layer of process. If it feels familiar, the team will go with it.

turns.inner_thought: To preserve the behavioral logic, I need a short calibration before the first planning session so people share the same frame and don't improvise their own version. And the team brief can't just be a note; they need an artifact set with examples so everyone starts from a common mental model. Otherwise any observations from the pilot will be noisy.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I would suggest a short calibration before the first planning session, and we should have a brief for the team so everyone goes in with the same mental model.

turns.inner_thought: I can own the brief. I'll make it a concise Confluence page and give a five-minute intro live during planning. That should be plenty. And if I finish it before Monday morning, plus the Jira template adjustments, then everything is ready by next Monday. No need to over-engineer onboarding for one squad.
turns.utterance: That's fine — I'll draft the brief for the team in Confluence and make sure it's in place so we're ready by next Monday. That should give us enough structure without turning this into a big rollout.

turns.inner_thought: I'll build worked examples that illustrate the Vickrey-style mechanism and the decision framing clearly. But the team needs to see those before Monday, ideally by Friday, so they aren't encountering the protocol cold in the room. 'Ready by next Monday' to me means participant-facing materials already circulated in advance.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I can prepare some examples for the brief, and I'd like us to circulate them ahead of time so people aren't seeing the mechanism cold on Monday.

turns.inner_thought: Responsibilities should stay simple: I'll handle Jira fields, planning agenda tweaks, and making sure the ceremony stays on schedule. Daniel can run the Vickrey round during planning and then a quick retro check-in afterward. As long as this remains bounded to planning plus a brief retro discussion, it's manageable.
turns.utterance: Okay, on responsibilities: I'll take Jira and the ceremony logistics, and you can facilitate the Vickrey round plus the retrospective check-in. That keeps ownership pretty clean.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I also need to include the pre-session framing and a more structured retrospective exercise on cooperation choices if this pilot is going to produce meaningful observations. I assume that's part of the two-sprint pilot already, so I don't need to re-litigate scope; I'll just fold it into my facilitation prep.
turns.utterance: Works for me. And for the pilot to be meaningful, I'll also set up the pre-session framing and a structured retrospective exercise around the cooperation choices.

turns.inner_thought: This sounds aligned enough. I'll summarize it in the lightest possible way so it doesn't start growing. From my perspective, we have a low-friction two-sprint pilot: brief in Confluence, Vickrey-style round in planning, short retro discussion, all set by Monday morning. Good.
turns.utterance: Great. So we're looking at a low-friction pilot for two sprints, with a brief for the team, a Vickrey-style round in planning, and a retro discussion, all ready by next Monday.

turns.inner_thought: I should make sure the facilitation materials and examples are solid and get them into review quickly, ideally before the weekend, so Monday starts with everyone primed. I still assume the brief includes the training artifact set and that the pilot scope includes the calibration and structured retro. I'll just move ahead on that basis.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. I'll flesh out the examples and facilitation materials, and we can review progress asynchronously before launch.
